meta.title: ppush — secure secret sharing
meta.description: Share passwords, confidential text and files through end-to-end encrypted, self-destructing links.
meta.homeDescription: Share a password, text or file as an end-to-end encrypted, self-destructing link. Zero-knowledge: the server never sees your secret, no account required.
meta.aboutDescription: How ppush works: zero-knowledge encryption in your browser, self-destructing links, view limits and tracking. Data hosted in France, delivered via Cloudflare.
meta.whyDescription: Pass on a password, a code or a confidential document without it lingering in your email or chats. Simple, free, no account needed.
meta.apiDocsDescription: ppush REST API: create and manage end-to-end encrypted, self-destructing secret links programmatically using personal access tokens.
meta.legalDescription: Legal notice for ppush: publisher, hosting, GDPR and LCEN compliance, data retention and contact for the secure secret-sharing service.
meta.privacyDescription: ppush privacy policy: data processed, legal bases, retention periods and your rights. Secrets are end-to-end encrypted and never readable by the server.
meta.loginDescription: Sign in to ppush to access your secret history, view tracking and larger file uploads. Passwordless sign-in with a passkey is supported.
meta.registerDescription: Create a free ppush account to see who opened your secrets, keep a history of your links, share larger files and enjoy longer retention.
meta.recoverDescription: Locked out of your ppush account? Submit an identity-verified recovery request. We never send reset emails — recovery is reviewed by a human.

entropy.title: Entropy in two minutes
entropy.s1: Entropy measures unpredictability, in bits. Each extra bit doubles the number of possibilities an attacker must try: 10 bits is about a thousand guesses; 40 bits, a trillion.
entropy.s2: ppush mixes your secret with a randomly drawn 256-bit key (AES-256-GCM). The result has no structure left: without the key, it is noise. Trying every key would take billions of billions of times the age of the universe.
entropy.s3: The key protects the journey. The password you share will be used elsewhere, though: its strength depends on its own entropy, the one shown by the meter under the field.
entropy.tableCaption: Time to try them all, at 100 billion guesses/s per card
entropy.tableNote: Generator passphrases: words + 2 digits + 1 symbol. This is the worst case: a stolen database where the password was stored as MD5, attacked with consumer graphics cards (RTX 4090, hashcat’s public benchmarks). A well-built site stores it with bcrypt or argon2, about half a million times slower to attack: 3 words then hold for over a century against one card. And online, login attempt limits make guessing impossible.
entropy.s4t: And where does ppush fit in?
entropy.s4: Our server only receives the entropy: the cloud. The key stays in your link, after the #, and is never sent to us. That is why we cannot read your secrets, even if asked to.
entropy.srcAnssi: ANSSI, multi-factor authentication and passwords (2021, in French)
entropy.srcCnil: CNIL, deliberation no. 2022-100 on passwords (in French)
entropy.tableAdvice: The default suits everyday use, all the more since a generated password is unique: even cracked, it opens only one door. For what really matters (main email, bank, password manager), aim for 80 bits, the threshold recommended by CNIL: 6 words.

tips.label: Tip
list: Use a unique password for every site — a breach on one shouldn't unlock the others.
A passphrase of 4–5 random words beats a short complex password — and it's easier to remember.
Length wins: every extra character makes a password exponentially harder to crack.
Never reuse your email password anywhere else — it's the master key to all your accounts.
Turn on two-factor authentication wherever you can; ppush supports it too.
Prefer a passkey over a password when offered — there's nothing to phish or leak.
A password manager remembers strong, unique passwords so you don't have to.
Sharing a password by email or chat? Send a ppush link instead — it self-destructs.
For the most sensitive secrets, set the link to expire after a single view.
The decryption key lives in the link's # fragment — it never reaches our server.
Add a passphrase to the link: one more layer, known only to the recipient.
Send the link and its passphrase through two different channels.
Beware of links you didn't expect — even a ppush link can be sent to trick you.
Check the address bar: phishing pages mimic real ones with look-alike domains.
With an account you keep a history of your links and see who opened them, and when.
Free account perks: bigger files, longer expiry, more views, and view tracking.
A short expiry limits the damage if a link ends up in the wrong hands.
We only ever store ciphertext — without the link, even we can't read your secret.
Rotate important passwords periodically, and immediately after any breach.
Don’t leave passwords on a sticky note: a password manager is far safer.
Public Wi-Fi is fine for ppush — the secret is encrypted before it leaves your browser.
The more views you allow, the more chances a secret has to leak. Keep it low.
Avoid personal info in passwords — names, birthdays and pets are easy to guess.
Treat a recovery code like a password: store it somewhere safe and private.
Once a link is destroyed or expired, its content is gone for good. By design.
Generate strong passwords right here with the built-in generator.
If a site emails you your password in clear text, that's a serious red flag.
Log out on shared computers, and let the link expire once it has been read.
A secret you no longer need is a risk you no longer want — let it expire.
Trust the source before you reveal: a link from a stranger may not be a gift.

recover.title: Trouble signing in?
recover.subtitle: Request a human-verified account recovery.
recover.noEmail: We never send reset emails — that's deliberate. Your account isn't tied to a recoverable inbox, which removes a whole class of takeover attacks.
recover.humanVerified: Recovery is reviewed by a human: an administrator verifies your identity before doing anything.
recover.prepareProof: Prepare your proof: the email you registered with, whether you have a passkey or 2FA, your approximate sign-up date, and details only the account owner would know.
recover.passkeyTip: The surest way to never get locked out: add a <link>passkey</link> — you can always sign back in without a password.
recover.messageLabel: Describe your situation and your proof
recover.messageHint: The more verifiable detail you give, the faster we can help.
recover.messagePlaceholder: What happened, and how you can prove the account is yours: passkey/2FA status, approximate sign-up date, recent links you created, devices/locations you usually sign in from…
recover.contactHint: Another channel to reach you, in case your account email isn't the best way. A human will get back to you — not an automated message.
recover.contactPlaceholder: e.g. a secondary email, a handle…
recover.genericError: Could not send your request. Please try again.
recover.sentBody: An administrator will review it and verify your identity before getting back to you. There is no automatic email — you'll be contacted.
recover.sentReminder: Keep your proof of identity ready, and don't create a duplicate request.
